Major technology corporations are approaching maximum borrowing boundaries within the global bond sector, Wells Fargo warns.

Market participants are penalizing individual debt offerings that surpass $25 billion.

Combined issuance from top hyperscalers, alongside data center developments by firms like Nvidia and SpaceX, has driven total volume to roughly $400 billion for the year.

The massive financial push by hyperscalers, cloud architecture firms, and data center operators to build AI infrastructure has hit structural limits in international debt markets, according to Wells Fargo.

Maureen O'Connor, global head of high-grade debt syndicate at Wells Fargo, characterized the recent trend as a distinct "supply shock" affecting the $15 trillion investment-grade landscape. Speaking on Bloomberg TV, O'Connor emphasized that the market is rapidly nearing its saturation ceiling.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Surging Corporate Bond Volumes

Primary tech hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle have collectively brought over $200 billion in corporate bonds to market within the current calendar year. When factoring in specialized data center funding initiatives from industry players like Nvidia Corp. and SpaceX, aggregate volume surges to approximately $400 billion, Wells Fargo noted.

According to O'Connor, bond offerings that eclipse the $25 billion threshold are now facing negative reactions in secondary trading. Consequently, financial advisors recommend that individual issuers limit their visits to the bond market to twice a year.

"We have definitely recognized a bit of a pivot point in and around about $25 billion per issuance being a bit of a pain point for investors," O'Connor stated during the broadcast. "It puts a little bit of a lid on how much these companies can actually borrow directly from the investment-grade market."

Looking ahead, O'Connor anticipates a structural shift in how firms secure capital for AI hardware components, projecting expanded use of off-balance-sheet financing models next year, specifically tailored for graphics processing units (GPUs) and tensor processing units (TPUs).

AMZN, GOOGL, MSFT Stock: Retail View

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was 'bearish' towards Amazon stock and was 'neutral' for Microsoft and Alphabet stock, with 'normal' to 'high' message volumes.

AMZN stock has gained 15%, Microsoft has added 8%, and Google has lost 4% year-to-date.

Key Takeaways

By Nov. 12, DBS had cut its Oracle price target to $290 from $310 and kept its Buy rating, which leaves 126% upside from the Nov. 11 close.

Oracle is 48% below its June high after a credit downgrade, negative free cash flow, a scrapped Tencent lease and Microsoft winding down a deal.

Analysts have raised estimates as the stock fell, so it trades at 15x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 21x.

DBS's $290 is 26x fiscal 2028 earnings. A rebound looks reasonable, but $290 within a year needs a re-rating Oracle hasn't earned yet.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) is 48% below its June high, and DBS still sees 126% upside, even after trimming its target. By Nov. 12, DBS's Andy Yu had cut his price target to $290 from $310 and kept his Buy rating.

The cut follows early-November reports that Oracle scrapped a Tencent chip lease and that Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle.

Funding Fears, Then Two Pulled Deals

The bill for the AI build came first. S&P cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB- in July, and Oracle's fiscal first-quarter report on Sept. 10 showed free cash flow of negative $5 billion on $28.5 billion of capital spending, and a finished $20 billion stock sale.

The two reports landed two days apart. The Financial Times reported on Nov. 4 that Oracle scrapped the $7 billion Tencent lease after US officials raised concerns. On Nov. 6, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft had spent recent months switching off rented Oracle servers that ran older Nvidia chips.

A Smaller Target, but Still a Big One

DBS's $290 is 23% above the Street's average target of $236. Bernstein's Mark Moerdler sits higher still: he kept his $325 target on Nov. 10, after rerunning his firm's 10-year forecast on management's new figures.

Oracle gave a path to positive free cash flow at its Oct. 28 Investor Day, and CFO Hilary Maxson restated it on CNBC on Nov. 10: "We're fully funded, cash flow positive in the second half of our 28, $30 billion plus free cash flow in 29." (Oracle's fiscal years end in May.)

Vancouver, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - November 12, 2026) - Oracle Commodity Holding Corp. (TSXV: ORCL) (OTCQB: ORLCF) ("Oracle" or the "Company") announces that it has increased the size of its non-brokered private placement (the "Offering"), previously announced on November 11, 2026, to an aggregate of up to 5,000,000 units (the "Units") at $0.03 per Unit, for gross proceeds of up to $150,000. Each Unit will consist of one common share of the Company (each, a "Share") and one transferable common share purchase warrant (each, a "Warrant"). Each Warrant will entitle the holder to purchase one additional Share at an exercise price of $0.06 for three years from the date of issuance.

Insiders of the Company (the "Insiders") are expected to subscribe for up to 2,500,000 Units for aggregate gross proceeds of up to $75,000. The issuance of Units to the Insiders is considered a related party transaction within the meaning of Multilateral Instrument 61-101 – Protection of Minority Security Holders in Special Transactions ("MI 61-101"). The Company anticipates relying on exemptions from the minority shareholder approval and formal valuation requirements applicable to "related-party transactions" under sections 5.5(a) and 5.7(1)(a), respectively, of MI 61-101, as neither the fair market value of the Units to be acquired by the participating Insiders nor the consideration to be paid by such Insiders are anticipated to exceed 25 percent of the Company's market capitalization. The Company will file a material change report in respect of the related party transaction.

The Company may elect to pay finders' fees to certain eligible finders in accordance with the policies of the TSX Venture Exchange.

The Offering is subject to certain conditions, including, but not limited to, the receipt of all necessary approvals, including the approval of the TSX Venture Exchange. All securities issued in connection with the Offering are subject to a statutory hold period of four months and one day from the date of issuance in accordance with applicable Canadian securities laws and the policies of the TSX Venture Exchange.

The Company intends to use the proceeds from the Offering for general working capital.

The Offering will not result in the creation of a new control person of the Company, and the Company is not aware of any undisclosed material information.

About Oracle Commodity Holding Corp.

Oracle Commodity Holding Corp. is a mining royalty company holding royalties on several precious metal and critical mineral mining projects.

China Hawk: Export Controls Have Cost Nvidia "Exactly Zero Sales." Congress Wants That to Change ©Mariia Demchenko from Getty Images and Billion Photos via Canva
Key Takeaways

The US is considering a rule that would stop Chinese AI companies from renting advanced chips in data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and other countries, and Congress looks likely to add chip provisions to this year's defense bill.

Chris McGuire, a China hawk, argues that export controls haven't cost NVIDIA any sales so far, because every chip it makes still finds a buyer.

NVIDIA's real exposure is Southeast Asia, where McGuire says $80 billion of AI chips went this year, and the same curbs would hit Oracle's Chinese cloud customers.

With its chips sold out and its stock at 14x forward earnings, NVIDIA looks less exposed to the curbs than Oracle does.

Washington wants to close the route Chinese AI companies use to reach NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) chips, and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) could get caught up in it too.

Chris McGuire was deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council from 2022 to 2024. He's now a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations. On this week's episode of Prof G Markets, he was asked whether the Megaspeed smuggling case could cut off a big chunk of NVIDIA's revenue. He said it's "the tip of the iceberg on the smuggling," but he's less worried about NVIDIA's sales:

"the export controls so far, I would argue, have cost NVIDIA exactly zero sales"

And McGuire wants the controls tighter.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia's Analyst Ratings

Southeast Asia is NVIDIA's real exposure

McGuire is right about the official numbers. Customers based in China, including Hong Kong, brought NVIDIA $19.7 billion of revenue in the year ended January 2026, down from $25.0 billion the year before. Management's outlook assumes no China data center compute revenue at all. NVIDIA also took a $4.5 billion charge on the H20, the chip it designed for China, and its total revenue still rose 65% that year to $215.9 billion.

But NVIDIA's China figures don't show where its chips end up. McGuire said trade data show $80 billion of AI chips went to Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia this year. That's about half of all the AI chips that don't go to the US. "And these are countries that don't have robust AI industries," he said. US companies run some of the data centers there, but others are cloud providers selling compute to China. The Information reported that Tencent, Alibaba and ByteDance have deals with data-center operators abroad that give them access to advanced NVIDIA chips.
